prompt.context: Our client is a global automobile manufacturer that has been losing money for several years in its North American division. The new CEO suspects a big reason may be the company's high degree of vertical integration. The client currently makes about 70% of its own parts, compared to 30–50% at its chief competitors.
prompt.question: The CEO has asked us to develop a cost-saving strategy around this issue. How would you approach this?

clarifying_info.q: How much of revenue goes toward parts-making operations?
clarifying_info.a: The client spends 35% of its North American revenues on parts-making operations.

clarifying_info.q: How much does the client buy externally?
clarifying_info.a: It buys (sources) another 10% of revenues from independent suppliers, most but not all of which are located in North America.

clarifying_info.q: How many plants does the client operate?
clarifying_info.a: Parts-making operations are spread over six divisions covering about 100 plants in the U.S. and Canada. The same parts are often made in several plants.

clarifying_info.q: What is the labor situation at the plants?
clarifying_info.a: All plants are unionized, with high labor costs and generally average (often poor) quality. Top UAW executives are split over the issue of give-backs.

clarifying_info.q: Is there excess capacity in the industry?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. There is excess capacity both in the client's own parts manufacturing plants and throughout the auto parts supplier industry.

clarifying_info.q: Would outside suppliers be interested in this business?
clarifying_info.a: Auto parts suppliers would be eager to win business from the client because it would reduce their dependency on the other two U.S. auto manufacturers.

framework: Identify the key hypothesis: the client could save $X millions by making only those parts where it has a competitive advantage or a strategic requirement
Analyze comparative costs: what it costs the client to make each part vs. what it would cost to buy from independent suppliers
Assess strategic value: which parts carry strategic importance (e.g., proprietary technology, competitive differentiation) that justifies making even at higher cost

Map each part on a 2x2: Cost-to-Make vs. Buy (low/high) × Strategic Value (low/high) — quadrant logic: low cost-to-make & high strategic value = Make; high cost-to-make & low strategic value = Buy; others = Attack Costs or Rationalize
Evaluate practicality and implementation: union dynamics, buy-in from client managers, consolidation of duplicate plants, standardization of parts across platforms
Benchmark: compare client's plants against each other (best current capabilities) and against external auto parts manufacturers
Get market quotes from potential suppliers globally for a broad cross-section of parts to establish market prices
Interview R&D, design, and engineering managers to determine which parts are strategically important and why
Assess consolidation opportunity: given excess capacity, evaluate moving parts currently made in multiple plants into a single plant for scale economies
Analyze cost chain and cost drivers, including standardization of parts across platforms and economies of scale

questions.prompt: What is the key hypothesis for this engagement?
questions.guidance: A strong hypothesis is a testable statement that, if true, has significant implications for the client. Expected answer: 'The client could save $X millions by making only those parts where it has a competitive advantage or a strategic requirement (i.e., a business reason to be in that part's manufacturing).'

questions.prompt: Assuming the hypothesis is true, what are the significant implications for the client?
questions.guidance: Look for logical soundness and creativity. Implications include: large cost savings potential (client spends 35% of NA revenue on parts-making); possible plant closures and workforce reductions; major union negotiations and potential labor conflict; need to develop/manage a broader external supplier base; risk of losing capabilities in strategically important parts; opportunity to redirect capital to core vehicle design and assembly competencies.

questions.prompt: How would you go about testing this hypothesis? Walk through your framework or work plan.
questions.guidance: At minimum the framework must cover: (1) Comparative costs — what it costs to make vs. buy each part; (2) Strategic value — which parts must be kept in-house regardless of cost. A stronger framework maps parts on the 2x2 matrix (Cost-to-Make vs. Buy vs. Strategic Value) and adds benchmarking, supplier quotes, stakeholder interviews, consolidation analysis, and a change-management plan covering unions and managers.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond the core make-vs-buy decision, what other levers could the client use to reduce costs in its parts operations?

categories.name: Cost reduction in existing plants
ideas: Consolidate duplicate parts production from multiple plants into fewer plants to gain scale
Standardize parts across vehicle platforms to increase volumes and reduce complexity
Renegotiate labor contracts / pursue UAW give-backs on wages, benefits, and retirement
Improve plant productivity through lean manufacturing or process improvement
Close or sell the least efficient plants

categories.name: Supplier strategy
ideas: Dual-source key components to create price competition among suppliers
Establish long-term agreements with preferred suppliers to secure volume discounts
Pursue global sourcing — leverage lower-cost suppliers outside North America
Help suppliers invest in capacity, reducing client's need to own manufacturing assets

categories.name: Strategic / structural
ideas: Spin off or sell parts divisions as an independent supplier company
Form a joint venture with a parts supplier to share costs and retain some strategic control
License proprietary part designs to outside suppliers while retaining IP
Focus in-house manufacturing only on parts with genuine competitive advantage (e.g., novel battery technology, safety-critical components)

categories.name: Change management & buy-in
ideas: Include union and client managers on the study team from the start to build buy-in
Sequence plant actions to minimize union confrontation — start with voluntary retirements
Communicate a clear long-term employment framework to reduce uncertainty

recommendation: Stop making parts where external suppliers can deliver equal or higher quality at lower cost and where there is no strategic reason to remain in-house; redirect that spend to suppliers
Retain in-house manufacturing only for parts with genuine competitive advantage or strategic necessity (e.g., proprietary powertrain or safety technology)
Consolidate remaining in-house production into fewer, higher-volume plants to improve quality and reduce unit costs
risks: Union resistance and potential labor actions could delay or block plant closures and workforce reductions
Loss of manufacturing knowledge in divested categories could create supplier dependency and future quality issues
Supplier industry excess capacity is temporary; long-term supply security must be managed
Speed of execution: too fast risks labor conflict; too slow leaves cost savings on the table
next_steps: Benchmark all 100 plants — cost per part and quality — against internal best practice and external suppliers
Collect binding quotes from qualified global suppliers for a representative sample of parts
Interview R&D and engineering leadership to finalize the strategic-necessity list
Build a transition roadmap including union negotiation timeline, plant wind-down sequencing, and supplier qualification milestones
